pos: v.t. (to demand as of right, to call for an account; rendering Hebrew darash, baqash, Greek aiteō, ekzēteō)
etymology: From Latin requirere, to seek again, to demand. In Scripture the verb belongs to God as Judge — He requires what He has a right to, and He requires it of named persons.
biblical_def: To require in Scripture is to demand by right, and God is nearly always the one requiring. Micah puts the whole moral law in the form of a question: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Mic 6:8). He requires an account proportioned to what was given: “unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more” (Luk 12:48) — privilege calculated as debt, not as advantage. He requires blood: after the flood He declares, “surely your blood of your lives will I require; at the hand of every beast will I require it, and at the hand of man” (Gen 9:5), the charter of human life's sanctity because man is made in God's image. And He requires the blood of the unwarned from the watchman who kept silent: “the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand” (Eze 3:18). What God requires, He will collect.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines require as to demand, to ask as of right and by authority; to claim as by right and authority; and to call to account for.
webster_full: REQUIRE, v.t. To demand; to ask as of right and by authority.
2. To claim; to render necessary by an imperative statute.
3. To ask as a favor; to request.
4. To call to account for.
5. To make necessary; to need; to demand.
scriptures: Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more.
Gen 9:5
And surely your blood of your lives will I require; at the hand of every beast will I require it, and at the hand of man; at the hand of every man's brother will I require the life of man.
Eze 3:18

When I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning, nor speakest to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand.
corruption_summary: Micah 6:8 has been detached from its context and made a summary of religion without atonement — a manageable ethic offered as an alternative to the sacrifice the same chapter assumes.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is quoted as though it abolished the need for blood: God does not want offerings, only justice, mercy, and humility. But Micah 6 opens with the LORD pleading a covenant lawsuit against Israel, and the question in verse 6 is what a man shall bring — calves, thousands of rams, his firstborn for his transgression. The answer of verse 8 does not cancel sacrifice; it exposes sacrifice offered by men who trample the poor, exactly as Isaiah 1 does. Reduce the verse to a slogan and it becomes what it was never meant to be: a religion of decent conduct with no propitiation and no Saviour, which leaves the covenant lawsuit unanswered.

Luke 12:48 and Ezekiel 3:18 then close the exits. Much given means much required, so the well-taught church member stands under a heavier reckoning than the pagan, not a lighter one. And the watchman who saw the sword and said nothing is charged with the blood, which is the most sobering statement in Scripture about the cost of a comfortable silence. God requires; the only question is whether a man has a Substitute when the account is called.
roots_summary: Hebrew darash (H1875), to seek, enquire, require, and baqash (H1245), to seek or demand; Greek aiteō (G154) and ekzēteō (G1567), to demand or require of.
roots_lines: Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, enquire, require an account; “what doth the LORD require of thee” (Mic 6:8) and “will I require” (Gen 9:5).
Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek, demand; “his blood will I require at thine hand” (Eze 3:18).
Greek aiteō (G154) — to ask, demand; the passive of Luk 12:48, “of him shall be much required.”
usage: “What doth the LORD require of thee” — asked inside a covenant lawsuit, not outside one.
“Unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required” — privilege reckoned as debt.
“His blood will I require at thine hand” — the cost of a comfortable silence.

pos: v.t. (to give back what is owed; rendering Hebrew shub in the causative, Greek apodidōmi)
etymology: From Latin reddere, to give back. To render is not to give a gift but to return a due — which is why Christ used it about taxes and Paul about vengeance.
biblical_def: To render is to give back what is owed, and the New Testament uses it to settle three accounts. Civil: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21) — two spheres, two debts, and neither dissolved into the other. Social: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour” (Rom 13:7) — a Christian pays what he owes to every authority, including the honour that costs nothing but pride. Personal: “See that none render evil for evil unto any man; but ever follow that which is good, both among yourselves, and to all men” (1Th 5:15) — the one debt the believer is forbidden to pay, because vengeance is a debt God has reserved to Himself. And devotional: “What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?” (Psa 116:12) — a question that cannot be answered in kind, and the psalmist's response is to take the cup of salvation and call on His name.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines render as to return, to pay back, to give in return, to restore, and to yield or give up.
webster_full: RENDER, v.t. To return; to pay back; as, to render good for evil.
2. To inflict, as a retribution.
3. To give on demand; to give; to assign.
4. To restore; to give back.
5. To surrender; to yield or give up the command of.
scriptures: They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Rom 13:7
Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
See that none render evil for evil unto any man; but ever follow that which is good, both among yourselves, and to all men.
What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?
corruption_summary: “Render unto Caesar” is used to build a wall between faith and public life — a private religion with no claim on the state — where Christ divided the debts without conceding a sphere.
corruption_paragraphs: The saying is regularly deployed to mean that religion belongs in one compartment and politics in another, which is a doctrine Christ did not teach and the dictionary rejects along with the Radical Two-Kingdoms position. He answered a trap about a coin bearing Caesar's image by pointing at the image, and then said render unto God the things that are God's — and man bears God's image. Caesar may have the coin; God has the man, including the man who is Caesar. That is a limit on the state, not a licence for it.

1 Thessalonians 5:15 marks the one debt a believer must leave unpaid. Rendering evil for evil is the most natural transaction in the world, and it is forbidden because Romans 12 has already assigned the account elsewhere: vengeance is Mine, I will repay, saith the Lord. And Psalm 116 shows what happens when a man tries to render to God on the same terms. He cannot; there is nothing to give back that was not first received; and so he lifts the cup of salvation, which is to receive again. The only rendering God accepts is worship.
roots_summary: Hebrew shub (H7725) in the causative, to bring back or repay; Greek apodidōmi (G591), to give back what is due — the verb of taxes, dues, and forbidden vengeance.
roots_lines: Greek apodidōmi (G591) — to give back, pay off, render what is owed; “render therefore unto Caesar” (Mat 22:21) and “render to all their dues” (Rom 13:7).
The same verb is used of God rendering to every man according to his deeds (Rom 2:6) — the final settling of accounts.
Hebrew shub (H7725) in the hiphil — to bring back, restore, repay; behind “what shall I render unto the LORD” (Psa 116:12).
usage: “Render therefore unto Caesar… and unto God” — two debts, and the image decides which.
“Render therefore to all their dues” — including honour, which costs only pride.
“See that none render evil for evil” — the one account reserved to God.

pos: n. & v. (profit, advantage; to acquire; rendering Hebrew betsa, Greek kerdos, kerdainō)
etymology: From the French gain, profit. Paul takes the merchant's ledger and reverses its columns — what was gain he counts loss, and dying itself he enters as profit.
biblical_def: Gain is profit, and the New Testament rewrites the ledger in which it is entered. Our Lord sets the maximum possible gain against the only asset that matters: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mar 8:36) — the largest imaginable acquisition, and it does not cover the cost. Paul applies the accounting to his own résumé: “what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ” (Php 3:7) — pedigree, zeal, and blameless law-keeping moved from the credit column to the debit. He then makes the boldest entry in the New Testament: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Php 1:21) — death itself booked as profit, because it delivers the only asset he holds. And he names the one investment that reliably yields: “godliness with contentment is great gain” (1Ti 6:6), written in the same paragraph that warns of men supposing that gain is godliness. The ledger is not abolished. It is corrected.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gain as profit, advantage, or interest; something obtained as an advantage; and unlawful advantage or lucre.
webster_full: GAIN, n. Profit; interest; something obtained as an advantage.
2. Unlawful advantage.
3. Overplus in computation; any thing opposed to loss.
GAIN, v.t. To obtain by industry or the employment of capital; to get as profit or advantage; to acquire.
2. To win; to obtain by superiority or success.
scriptures: Mar 8:36
For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
Php 3:7
But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ.
Php 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
But godliness with contentment is great gain.
corruption_summary: Prosperity teaching inverts 1 Timothy 6 exactly, supposing that gain is godliness — the error Paul names in the verses just before he calls contentment the real profit.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul describes men of corrupt minds “supposing that gain is godliness” and tells Timothy to withdraw himself from such. The prosperity gospel, in its crude and its respectable forms alike, is that supposition organised: faith as an instrument of return, giving as seed capital, and material increase as evidence of divine favour. Paul's correction is not that money is evil but that the equation runs the other way — godliness with contentment is the gain, and the man who has that has profited whatever his balance shows. He adds the reason: we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.

Mark 8:36 supplies the arithmetic at the largest scale, and it is worth doing slowly. A man may acquire everything — the whole world, every asset, without exception — and the exchange still ruins him, because the thing traded away is not replaceable and no residual value remains. Philippians 1:21 is the same equation solved by a man who owns nothing and expects execution: to die is gain. Only one of those two men is investing wisely, and it is not the one with the world.
roots_summary: Hebrew betsa (H1215), unjust gain or profit; Greek kerdos (G2771), gain, and kerdainō (G2770), to gain — the merchant's vocabulary turned on the soul.
roots_lines: Hebrew betsa (H1215) — profit, plunder, dishonest gain; the covetousness an elder must be free of (compare 1Ti 3:3).
Greek kerdainō (G2770) — to gain, win; “gain the whole world” (Mar 8:36) and Paul gaining men for Christ (1Co 9:19).
Greek porismos (G4200) — a means of gain; the word behind “supposing that gain is godliness” and “godliness with contentment is great gain” (1Ti 6:5-6).
usage: “What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world” — the largest possible acquisition, and still short.
“What things were gain to me, those I counted loss” — the columns reversed.
“Godliness with contentment is great gain” — the only reliable yield.

pos: n. (an account given; reputation; rendering Hebrew shemuah, Greek akoē, marturia)
etymology: From Latin reportare, to carry back. In Scripture a report is either the gospel message carried to men, or a man's reputation carried among them.
biblical_def: Report in the Authorized Version means two things, and both matter. First, a message carried: Isaiah's great question, “Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?” (Isa 53:1) — quoted by John and by Paul of the general unbelief that met the preaching of Christ, and answered in Romans 10 with the doctrine that faith cometh by hearing. Second, a man's standing among those who know him. The seven chosen to serve tables had to be “men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3) — character attested before gifts are deployed. An elder “must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (1Ti 3:7) — the testimony of unbelieving neighbours counting as a qualification for office. And the whole company of the faithful is summed up in it: “For by it the elders obtained a good report” (Heb 11:2) — by faith, and the report they obtained was God's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines report as an account returned, a statement of facts given in reply; rumor; and public character or reputation.
webster_full: REPORT, v.t. To bear or bring back an answer, or to relate what has been discovered by a person sent to examine.
2. To give an account of; to relate; to tell.
3. To give an official account or statement.
REPORT, n. An account returned; a statement or relation of facts given in reply to inquiry.
2. Rumor; common fame; story circulated. 3. Repute; public character.
scriptures: Isa 53:1
Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?
Act 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.
Heb 11:2
For by it the elders obtained a good report.
corruption_summary: Reputation among outsiders has been dismissed as people-pleasing, but Paul made it an eldership qualification — while the report a church actually cultivates is too often platform rather than character.
corruption_paragraphs: Two failures run in opposite directions. The first shrugs off outside opinion entirely: what unbelievers think of a leader is held to be irrelevant, or even a badge of faithfulness when it is bad. 1 Timothy 3:7 forbids that shrug — a man must have a good report of them which are without, and Paul attaches a reason, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. The neighbours who watch a man pay his bills, treat his wife, and keep his word are competent witnesses to the things eldership requires.

The second failure cultivates the wrong report. Where a ministry is built on reach, the report that matters becomes visibility, and character verification is postponed until a scandal enforces it. Acts 6 puts the order the other way round for a job as ordinary as distributing food: honest report first, then appointment. And Hebrews 11 names the only report finally worth obtaining — it was obtained by faith, and the One giving it is not the crowd.
roots_summary: Hebrew shemuah (H8052), a thing heard, a report; Greek akoē (G189), the thing heard, and martureō (G3140), to bear witness — the message carried and the character attested.
roots_lines: Hebrew shemuah (H8052) — a report, tidings, thing heard; “who hath believed our report?” (Isa 53:1).
Greek akoē (G189) — hearing, the thing heard; John quotes Isaiah's report with this word (Joh 12:38), and Rom 10:17 makes faith come by it.
Greek martureō (G3140) — to bear witness, be well reported of; the honest report of Act 6:3 and the good report of Heb 11:2.
usage: “Who hath believed our report?” — the prophet's question about his own generation, and ours.
“Men of honest report” — character verified before a table is served.
“By it the elders obtained a good report” — and the One reporting is God.

pos: n. pl. (things done, acts; rendering Hebrew ma'aseh, Greek erga, praxeis)
etymology: Saxon dæd, from don, to do. Scripture never treats deeds as unimportant — it denies that they can justify while insisting they will be judged.
biblical_def: Deeds are things done, and Scripture holds two truths about them that must never be separated. First, they cannot justify: “Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin” (Rom 3:20) — the law's function toward the sinner is diagnostic, not curative. Second, they reveal and will be judged: “this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil” (Joh 3:19) — men do not reject Christ for want of evidence but because of what they are doing in the dark. Deeds belong to the old man and are put off with him: “Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds” (Col 3:9). And Christ commends a church for a specific hatred: “this thou hast, that thou hatest the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate” (Rev 2:6) — the risen Lord naming a party by name and telling a congregation He shares their hatred of what it does.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deed as that which is done, acted or effected; an act, an achievement; and in law, a written instrument sealed and delivered.
webster_full: DEED, n. That which is done, acted or effected; an act; a fact; a word of extensive application, including whatever is done, good or bad, great or small.
2. Exploit; achievement.
3. Power of action; agency.
4. In law, a writing containing some contract or agreement, and the evidence of its execution.
scriptures: Rom 3:20
Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.
Joh 3:19
And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.
Col 3:9
Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds;
Rev 2:6
But this thou hast, that thou hatest the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.
corruption_summary: The two biblical truths about deeds are habitually split — one side making works the ground of acceptance, the other treating conduct as irrelevant once grace is professed.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome, and every moralism that resembles it, makes deeds a component of justification, so that a sinner is finally accepted partly on the basis of what grace has enabled him to do. Paul closes that door: by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified. Antinomianism runs out the opposite door, concluding that if deeds cannot justify they do not matter, and produces professing Christians whose lives are unchanged and untroubled by it. The Confession holds both hands open at once — faith alone justifies, and the faith that justifies is never alone.

John 3:19 explains why the argument is rarely settled by argument. Men loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil: unbelief has a moral root, not merely an intellectual one, and every man knows what he is protecting. Revelation 2:6 then shows the other side, the risen Christ commending a congregation for hating the deeds of a named party. A church with no capacity for that hatred has not become gracious; it has stopped being able to see in the light it claims to walk in.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'aseh (H4639), a work or deed; Greek erga (G2041), works, and praxeis (G4234), deeds or practices — unable to justify, certain to be judged.
roots_lines: Greek erga (G2041) — works, deeds; “the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:20) and “their deeds were evil” (Joh 3:19).
Greek praxeis (G4234) — deeds, practices, habitual doings; the old man with his deeds (Col 3:9).
Hebrew ma'aseh (H4639) — work, deed, act; used of God's works of creation and of man's works brought into judgment (Ecc 12:14).
usage: “By the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified” — the law diagnoses, it does not cure.
“Because their deeds were evil” — unbelief with a moral root.
“Thou hatest the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate” — a hatred Christ commends.

pos: v.t. & n. (to employ, to make service of; rendering Greek chraomai, chrēsis)
etymology: From Latin uti, to employ. Scripture's concern is almost never whether a thing may be used but whether it is being used lawfully and without abuse.
biblical_def: Use in the New Testament is a moral category: the question is not whether a thing is employed but how. The law is a case in point: “we know that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully” (1Ti 1:8) — a good instrument may be handled unlawfully, which is exactly what the false teachers of Ephesus were doing with it. The world is another: “they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away” (1Co 7:31) — the Christian is not withdrawn from creation but holds it loosely, because its arrangement is temporary. Hospitality is commanded as a use of one's home with a warning about the spirit of it: “Use hospitality one to another without grudging” (1Pe 4:9). And our Lord names the worst kind of use, and what to do about it: pray for “them which despitefully use you, and persecute you” (Mat 5:44). Being used badly by others is one of the certainties of a Christian life; the response is prescribed, and it is prayer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines use as the act of employing any thing, application, employment for the attainment of some purpose; and usage, custom, or practice.
webster_full: USE, n. The act of employing any thing, or of applying it to a purpose.
2. Employment; application of any thing to a purpose, good or bad.
3. Advantage received; profit; benefit.
USE, v.t. To employ; to handle or move for some purpose.
2. To make use of; to convert to one's service. 3. To treat or behave towards.
scriptures: But we know that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully;
And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
Mat 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
corruption_summary: The law is used unlawfully in two directions at once — as a ladder for the self-righteous, and as a whip laid on believers whom Christ has already justified.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul says the law is good if a man use it lawfully, and then names its lawful use: it is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient — that is, it is given to expose sin and drive the sinner to Christ. It is used unlawfully when a moralist climbs it, treating the commandments as a scale on which he may score well enough. It is used unlawfully again when a preacher lays it on the consciences of justified believers as though their standing depended on their performance. The same good instrument, handled two wrong ways, produces pride in one man and despair in another.

1 Corinthians 7:31 gives the corresponding rule for everything else. Use the world, as not abusing it: neither the asceticism that treats created things as inherently defiling, nor the worldliness that treats them as permanent. The clause supplies the reason — the fashion of this world passeth away — so the grip is loosened by eschatology, not by contempt. And 1 Peter 4:9 shows the ordinary shape of a rightly used possession: a door opened to a brother, and no grumbling about it afterward.
roots_summary: Greek chraomai (G5530), to use or employ, and chrēsis (G5540), use — with katachraomai (G2710), to use up or abuse, marking the boundary.
roots_lines: Greek chraomai (G5530) — to use, employ, deal with; “if a man use it lawfully” (1Ti 1:8).
Greek katachraomai (G2710) — to use to the full, misuse, abuse; “as not abusing it” (1Co 7:31).
Greek epēreazō (G1908) — to insult, treat despitefully; “them which despitefully use you” (Mat 5:44).
usage: “The law is good, if a man use it lawfully” — a good instrument, wrongly handled.
“They that use this world, as not abusing it” — a loosened grip, on eschatological grounds.
“Use hospitality one to another without grudging” — the door opened, and no complaint after.

pos: v.t. & adj. (to set apart, to divide; rendering Hebrew badal, nazar, Greek aphorizō, chōrizō)
etymology: From Latin separare, to put apart. The same root gives us holy in its practical sense: what is separated to God, and what sin separates from Him.
biblical_def: To separate is to set apart, and Scripture uses it for three separations: one that sin makes, one that God commands, and one that cannot happen. Sin's separation is stated flatly by Isaiah: “your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear” (Isa 59:2) — unanswered prayer traced to a cause. God's commanded separation is the church's distinctness: “come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you” (2Co 6:17). There is also a separation to a work rather than merely from a defilement: “the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them” (Act 13:2) — the first missionary sending, and the Spirit does the separating. And then the separation that is impossible: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Rom 8:35). Paul lists the strongest candidates and dismisses them all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines separate as to disunite, to divide, to sever; to set apart for a particular purpose; and as being detached, disconnected, or holy.
webster_full: SEPARATE, v.t. To disunite; to divide; to sever; to part, in almost any manner.
2. To set apart; to designate for a particular service.
3. To disconnect; as, to separate a man from his friends.
SEPARATE, a. Divided from the rest; being parted from another.
2. Unconnected; not united; disjoined. 3. Disunited from the body; incorporeal.
scriptures: Isa 59:2
But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Act 13:2
As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.
Rom 8:35
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
corruption_summary: Separation is treated either as a sectarian instinct to be outgrown or as a badge of superiority to be worn, when Scripture makes it a separation unto God and a work of the Spirit before it is a stance toward men.
corruption_paragraphs: One failure abandons the doctrine: a church so anxious about seeming narrow that it cannot say touch not the unclean thing about anything, and so becomes indistinguishable from the culture it hoped to reach. The other failure makes separation the whole of holiness — endless dividing over ever smaller matters, with the boundary itself as the object of devotion. 2 Corinthians 6 gives the promise that governs the command: and I will receive you. Separation from is always for the sake of separation to; where the second is missing, the first hardens into pride.

Acts 13 keeps the initiative where it belongs. The Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul — the church fasted and prayed and laid on hands, but the separating was God's and the men were separated to a work, not merely out of a company. And Romans 8:35 sets the outer boundary of the whole doctrine: sin separates, God separates, but nothing separates the believer from the love of Christ. The list Paul gives is not of trivia but of the worst things that happen to Christians, and he calls them all insufficient.
roots_summary: Hebrew badal (H914), to divide or separate, and nazar (H5144), to consecrate by separation; Greek aphorizō (G873), to mark off, and chōrizō (G5563), to put asunder.
roots_lines: Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, separate; used of God dividing light from darkness and Israel from the nations (Lev 20:24).
Greek aphorizō (G873) — to mark off by boundaries, set apart; “be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) and “separate me Barnabas and Saul” (Act 13:2).
Greek chōrizō (G5563) — to put apart, sever; “who shall separate us from the love of Christ” (Rom 8:35).
usage: “Your iniquities have separated between you and your God” — unanswered prayer, with a cause.
“Come out from among them, and be ye separate… and I will receive you” — separated from, unto Him.
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” — the list, and the answer.

pos: v.t. (to follow after with intent to overtake; rendering Hebrew radaph, Greek diōkō)
etymology: From Latin prosequi, to follow after. The same Hebrew verb serves for hunting an enemy and for chasing after peace — the intensity is the point.
biblical_def: To pursue is to follow hard after something with intent to overtake it, and Scripture makes the same verb serve for war and for holiness. David asks whether to give chase and is answered specifically: “Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all” (1Sa 30:8) — the pursuit authorised and its outcome promised before a step is taken. The psalmist commands the same energy toward an unlikely quarry: “Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it” (Psa 34:14) — peace does not arrive by drifting; it is hunted. Amos records the pursuit that damns a nation: Edom “did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever” (Amo 1:11). And Proverbs describes the pursuit that exists only in a guilty imagination: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pursue as to follow with a view to overtake; to chase; and to seek, to use measures to obtain, as to pursue peace or a course of conduct.
webster_full: PURSUE, v.t. To follow; to go or proceed after or in a like direction.
2. To take and persist in measures to obtain; as, to pursue a remedy at law.
3. To prosecute; to continue.
4. To follow as an example; to imitate.
5. To follow with enmity; to persecute.
scriptures: And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all.
Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.
Amo 1:11

Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever:
Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
corruption_summary: Peace is imagined as the absence of conflict that settles when people stop fighting, where the psalm makes it a quarry to be chased — and Romans adds the qualifier as much as lieth in you.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 34:14 uses a verb of hot pursuit, and it is worth noticing what precedes it: depart from evil, and do good. Peace is not pursued by avoidance, silence, or the pretence that nothing is wrong; it is pursued by leaving sin and doing good to the person one is at odds with. The passive substitute — waiting for tension to subside, calling distance reconciliation — is what Scripture nowhere commends. Matthew 5 sends the offended man and Matthew 18 sends the offender, so that on either reading somebody is walking.

Amos 1:11 shows the pursuit that runs the other way and the four things that make it damnable: he pursued, cast off pity, tore perpetually, and kept his wrath for ever. Grievance maintained across generations is not a lesser sin in God's reckoning; it is the charge on which Edom was judged. Proverbs 28:1 then adds the strange freedom of a clear conscience — the wicked flee with nobody behind them, and the righteous, who have real enemies, are bold as a lion.
roots_summary: Hebrew radaph (H7291), to pursue, chase, persecute; Greek diōkō (G1377), to pursue or persecute — one verb for hunting an enemy and for chasing peace.
roots_lines: Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue, chase, persecute; “seek peace, and pursue it” (Psa 34:14) and Edom pursuing his brother (Amo 1:11).
Greek diōkō (G1377) — to pursue, press toward, persecute; Paul pressing toward the mark (Php 3:14) and “follow peace with all men” (Heb 12:14).
The double sense is deliberate: the energy a man spends persecuting is the energy Scripture redirects toward peace and holiness.
usage: “Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them” — the chase authorised and its end promised.
“Seek peace, and pursue it” — peace hunted, not awaited.
“The wicked flee when no man pursueth” — a chase that exists only in the conscience.

pos: v.t. (to prohibit, to command not to do; rendering Greek kōluō, and in the oath-formula mē genoito)
etymology: Saxon forbeodan, to command against. The Authorized Version's God forbid renders a Greek phrase containing no word for God — a strong idiomatic let it not be.
biblical_def: To forbid is to prohibit, and the New Testament records both a forbidding Christ rebukes and forbiddings He commands. He rebukes the disciples for it: “Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God” (Mar 10:14) — the men guarding His time were the obstacle. Peter uses it to end an argument about Gentile converts: “Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?” (Act 10:47). Paul closes his long correction of Corinthian disorder without overreaching: “covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues” (1Co 14:39) — regulating what he would not prohibit. And the phrase God forbid, used fifteen times in the Authorized Version, carries Paul's strongest denials, none stronger than this: “God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world” (Gal 6:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forbid as to prohibit, to interdict, to command to forbear or not to do; to oppose, hinder, or obstruct.
webster_full: FORBID, v.t. To prohibit; to interdict; to command to forbear or not to do.
2. To command not to enter; to hinder from approach.
3. To oppose; to hinder; to obstruct.
4. To accurse; to blast.
FORBIDDEN, pp. Prohibited; interdicted.
scriptures: But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.
Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?
Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues.
Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
corruption_summary: Mark 10:14 is used to argue for infant baptism and, more broadly, to forbid the church any boundary at all — but the passage is about blessing children, and Christ Himself forbids a great deal elsewhere.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary holds believer's baptism by immersion, and Mark 10 does not overturn it: children are brought to Christ, He takes them up in His arms, puts His hands upon them and blesses them, and no water appears in the account. The verse is nevertheless one of the most cited in paedobaptist argument and one of the most quoted in a wider modern use — that Christ's only recorded rebuke about access proves the church should never fence anything. Both readings ask the verse to carry a load it does not bear. What it does establish is real and is often neglected: children are to be brought, welcomed, taught, and blessed, and a congregation that treats them as an interruption is doing precisely what the disciples did.

The other half of the word is Paul's God forbid, and it is the language of a man who knows exactly where the fences are. Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. Is the law sin? God forbid. Shall I glory in anything but the cross? God forbid. The Authorized Version's idiom is stronger than the Greek is literally, and it is a good translation, because Paul is invoking the unthinkable. A church with no forbidding left in it has lost the vocabulary of that verse.
roots_summary: Greek kōluō (G2967), to hinder, prevent, forbid; and mē genoito (G3361 with G1096), literally may it not be, rendered God forbid in the Authorized Version.
roots_lines: Greek kōluō (G2967) — to hinder, restrain, forbid; “forbid them not” (Mar 10:14) and “can any man forbid water” (Act 10:47).
Greek mē genoito — an emphatic optative of rejection, let it not be; rendered God forbid fifteen times, chiefly in Romans and Galatians.
The idiom is inherited from the Septuagint, where it renders a similar Hebrew formula of horrified refusal (compare Gen 44:7).
usage: “Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not” — the gatekeepers rebuked.
“Can any man forbid water” — the argument ended by an accomplished fact.
“God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross” — Paul's strongest form of denial.

pos: v.t. (to greet, to wish health to; rendering Greek aspazomai)
etymology: From Latin salutare, to wish health, from salus, health. A New Testament salutation is a small act with real weight — which is why Paul filled a whole chapter with them.
biblical_def: To salute is to greet, and the New Testament treats greeting as a genuine Christian duty rather than a formality. Paul ends Romans with a roll of names and a command: “Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you” (Rom 16:16) — a chapter of greetings preserved in the canon, which is Scripture's own estimate of how much particular people matter. Christ sends His disciples out with instructions on it: “when ye come into an house, salute it” (Mat 10:12), the greeting carrying a real peace that either rests on the house or returns. He also names the limit of natural courtesy: “if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so?” (Mat 5:47) — greeting one's own circle is not virtue, it is instinct. And from prison Paul relays greetings on behalf of others: “Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas” (Col 4:10). Fellowship keeps its manners in a cell.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines salute as to greet, to hail, to address with expressions of kind wishes, and to wish health or safety to a person on meeting.
webster_full: SALUTE, v.t. To greet; to hail; to address with expressions of kind wishes.
2. To please; to gratify.
3. To kiss.
SALUTE, n. The act of expressing kind wishes or respect; salutation; greeting.
SALUTATION, n. The act of saluting; a greeting; the act of paying respect or reverence by the customary words or actions.
scriptures: Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you.
And when ye come into an house, salute it.
Mat 5:47
And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so?
Col 4:10
Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas, (touching whom ye received commandments: if he come unto you, receive him;)
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What it recovers is the weight Scripture puts on ordinary greeting — a duty of love now largely displaced by distracted acknowledgement.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody is arguing about the word salute. What has quietly changed is the practice: greeting has thinned into a nod given while looking elsewhere, and a congregation can pass a whole Sunday in which no one is actually addressed by name.

The principle to recover is how seriously the New Testament takes it. Romans 16 is twenty-four verses of names, and the Spirit saw fit to preserve every one — Phebe, Priscilla and Aquila, Epaenetus, Mary who bestowed much labour on us. Christ's test in Matthew 5:47 is sharper still: greeting only one's own brethren is what publicans do, and the standard for a Christian is the visitor, the awkward member, and the one nobody has spoken to yet. Paul, in chains, still sent greetings from Aristarchus and Marcus. It costs almost nothing and it is nearly the whole visible substance of fellowship.
roots_summary: Greek aspazomai (G782), to greet, welcome, embrace — the standard verb of New Testament salutation, and the verb of the holy kiss.
roots_lines: Greek aspazomai (G782) — to greet, salute, welcome; used some sixty times, and twenty-one times in Romans 16 alone.
Greek aspasmos (G783) — a salutation; the greeting the scribes loved in the markets (Mar 12:38), a warning against greeting as display.
The holy kiss (Rom 16:16; 1Th 5:26) is the cultural form; the abiding command is genuine, particular, personal greeting within the body.
usage: “Salute one another with an holy kiss” — a command, not a courtesy.
“When ye come into an house, salute it” — the greeting carries a real peace.
“If ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others?” — the standard is the stranger.
